clinical_knowledge.topic: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addisonian Crisis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addisonian Crisis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Immediate IV Hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, followed by 50 mg IV q6h, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe dizziness, weakness, nausea, and hyperpigmentation of skin for 3 weeks

Key HPI features: 42M presents with 3-week worsening fatigue, profound orthostatic dizziness, anorexia, weight loss, and darkening of skin over knuckles and buccal mucosa. Arrives in emergency department feeling faint after mild gastroenteritis.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 112, BP 84/50 (orthostatic drop to 68/40). Hyperpigmented palmar creases and gingival mucosa. Bloods: Na 126 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Glucose 62 mg/dL, Urea 45 mg/dL. Random serum cortisol < 3 ug/dL with elevated ACTH (>500 pg/mL).
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addisonian Crisis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Sepsis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fainting with recent illness in a known autoimmune patient — treat as Addisonian crisis and give steroids immediately.
management_principles: Immediate IV Hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, followed by 50 mg IV q6h
Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation with 5% dextrose for hypoglycemia
Once stable, transition to maintenance oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 42M with polyglandular autoimmune tendencies presenting with subacute fatigue, orthostatic syncope, anorexia, and diffuse hyperpigmentation, worsening acutely into adrenal crisis.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 112, BP 84/50 (orthostatic drop to 68/40). Hyperpigmented palmar creases and gingival mucosa. Bloods: Na 126 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Glucose 62 mg/dL, Urea 45 mg/dL. Random serum cortisol < 3 ug/dL with elevated ACTH (>500 pg/mL).
reference_soap.assessment: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease) presenting in acute Addisonian Crisis.
reference_soap.plan: Immediate IV Hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, followed by 50 mg IV q6h. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation with 5% dextrose for hypoglycemia. Once stable, transition to maintenance oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Educate on steroid sick-day rules and emergency alert bracelet.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical and laboratory triad of acute Addisonian crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia)
Understand the pathophysiology of ACTH-mediated mucosal/skin hyperpigmentation
Implement emergent life-saving IV glucocorticoid and fluid therapy before lab confirmation
Educate patient thoroughly on lifelong glucocorticoid dosing and 'sick-day rules'

teaching.one_liner: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands causes chronic cortisol deficiency, presenting with fatigue, weight loss, and dark hyperpigmentation of the skin — and can decompensate into a life-threatening crisis during minor illness.
red_flags: Fainting with recent illness in a known autoimmune patient — treat as Addisonian crisis and give steroids immediately

history.answer: I feel terribly dizzy, exhausted, and weak, and I passed out twice at home today.
It feels like I am going to black out and faint, not like the room is spinning around me.
I have felt run down and dizzy for about three weeks, but it became much worse over the last two days.
The severe faintness hits me for a couple of minutes whenever I sit or stand, but the deep weakness is constant.
Standing up or getting out of bed brings on the dizziness and makes everything go dark, while lying flat helps.
I have felt nauseous for three weeks and threw up twice yesterday.
No, my hearing is completely fine, and I don't have any ringing or plugged feeling in my ears.
No, I haven't had double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, or any weakness or numbness in my face or limbs.
No severe headache or stiff neck at all, just a vague foggy feeling when I try to stand.
My heart beats fast when I feel faint, but I haven't had any chest pain or tightness.
I had a mild stomach flu with a bit of diarrhea two days ago, and I have felt completely drained ever since.
I had some watery diarrhea two days ago and haven't been able to eat or drink much, but no black or bloody stools.
No, I do not have diabetes and I don't take any insulin or blood sugar medicines.
No, I have never had migraines, and bright lights or loud noises don't bother me.
I don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, irregular heartbeats, or a history of stroke, and I don't smoke.
No, I have not started or changed any blood pressure drugs, water pills, sedatives, or seizure medications.
I am very worried because of how weak I am, but this is physical weakness rather than anxiety or panic.
My skin has turned noticeably darker over the past few weeks, especially on my knuckles and hands, even though I haven't been out in the sun.
I have had no appetite for the past three weeks and lost about four kilograms without trying.
I have Hashimoto's underactive thyroid and vitiligo with patchy skin, but no other chronic illnesses.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been hospitalized before.
I take levothyroxine 100 micrograms once every morning for my thyroid.
I don't have any allergies to medications or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I rarely drink, maybe one beer a month, and I haven't had anything to drink recently.
I work as a software engineer from home and live with my wife.
My mother has an underactive thyroid and rheumatoid arthritis, but nobody has had early heart attacks or strokes.
I think my blood pressure is dropping dangerously low every time I try to get up.
I am terrified because I collapsed twice today and can barely keep myself upright.
I want to receive IV fluids and immediate treatment so my body can stabilize and I stop fainting.

exam.finding: Chronically ill and lethargic male lying flat, appearing markedly fatigued and dehydrated with a weak voice.
Supine blood pressure 84/50 mmHg, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8 C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Blood pressure drops markedly to 68/40 mmHg upon sitting upright with pulse increasing to 126 beats per minute, precipitating severe lightheadedness.
Diffuse hyperpigmentation prominent across knuckles, extensor surfaces, and palmar creases, alongside scattered patches of vitiligo; skin turgor is noticeably reduced.
Patchy bluish-black hyperpigmentation on the buccal mucosa and gingiva, with dry mucous membranes and normal pharynx.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; extraocular movements are intact without resting or gaze-evoked nystagmus.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft with mild non-specific generalized tenderness, without guarding, rebound tenderness, or organomegaly.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial expression and clear speech.
No spontaneous, gaze-evoked, or positional nystagmus; head impulse test is normal.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements are intact; Romberg and tandem walking cannot be performed due to severe orthostatic lightheadedness.
